segments.text: For a moment, let's leave my fortifications aside.
In front of you is Palazzo Pretorio.
No, this building isn't my work.
Its oldest part dates from the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, before I arrived.
Look at the façade: the great pillars, the pointed arches, and that yellowish ochre stone you should be starting to recognise by now.
Verrucano.
A building doesn't come through centuries of history without changing.
I did warn you.
And this palace is an excellent example.
Its original purpose isn't entirely certain. It may have been connected with the power the archbishops of Pisa exercised over Vicopisano.
But its history becomes much clearer after the Florentine conquest of fourteen hundred and six.
A few years later, in fourteen eleven, the building was chosen as the seat of the Vicario.
The Vicario wasn't the town's mayor.
He represented the Florentine government: he administered the territory and dispensed justice in Florence's name.
From then on, the palace housed his offices, his residence…
and the prisons as well.
In other words, the same building was used to govern the territory, administer justice and, when necessary…
lock someone up.
Now, though, look at the coats of arms on the walls.
Almost fifty survive in the palace, some even from the Florentine workshops of the Della Robbia family.
From the fifteenth century onwards, each Vicario left his own coat of arms here.
A name.
A family.
A record of his time in Vicopisano.
And for me, there's something particularly interesting about these coats of arms.
They tell me what happened after my lifetime.
The Florentine Republic was followed by the Medici.
Then the House of Lorraine.
The Vicario's powers were gradually reduced, until the office was abolished in eighteen forty-eight.
Four centuries of government…
summed up on a wall.
But it wasn't just the rulers of Vicopisano who were changing.
Even the landscape changed.
Remember the Arno and the Serezza, the two waterways I told you about at the start of our walk?
When I arrived, the Arno flowed much closer to the town.
It formed a great bend and, together with the Serezza, had helped make Vicopisano a strategic place for trade, transport and defence for centuries.
Then, in the sixteenth century, the Medici decided to intervene.
From fifteen sixty onwards, the Arno's course was straightened and moved further from the walls, towards the route it still follows today.
The Serezza was altered too, to reach the river's new course and keep draining the waters from Lake Bientina.
Put simply…
the water that had helped Vicopisano prosper no longer flowed where it once had.
And that changed the town's role as well.
Agriculture became increasingly important.
But Vicopisano remained an important administrative centre, home to the Vicario, the court and the Florentine chancery.
I must admit:
for someone like me, used to altering walls, towers and passageways…
it's quite something to discover that here they went as far as changing the course of a river.
Clearly, history doesn't leave its mark only on buildings.
Sometimes it leaves its mark on the whole landscape.
It would be foolish to return to Vicopisano, bore you with nothing but my own work…
and overlook everything the town has lived through without me.
Now, though, we can return to something I know rather better.
Our next stop will finally bring us to the Rocca.
Allow me another little moment of well-earned pride.
